title: Freedomland
full_review:
In 1936, Luise Rainer won her first of two Academy Awards for her solitary emoting over the phone in "The Great Ziegfeld." If Oscars voters still reward such histrionics (and why not?), both Julianne Moore and Edie Falco can dust off their mantles right now, for each gets to deliver a knockout monologue.

Otherwise, though, "Freedomland" (Columbia) is an overheated, not to mention grim, melodrama that doesn't quite work.

The time is 1999, the place a predominantly African-American housing project in fictional Dempsy, N.J. Police detective Lorenzo Council (Samuel L. Jackson) has his hands full, keeping the peace between the project's residents and the white police force in the neighboring blue-collar town of Gannon.

When the film begins, a dazed working-class woman from Gannon, Brenda Martin (Moore in her grittiest performance yet), who has a job in an after-school program in the project, wanders into a hospital with bloodied hands. She claims she was driving near the project and was forced to get out of her car at gunpoint, thrown down to the ground, and the assailant drove off in her car with her 4-year-old boy in the back seat.

The veteran Lorenzo is assigned to protect her and get to the bottom of the abduction, though he is convinced Brenda -- who once had a drug problem -- is concealing the full truth. Despite his reservations about her, he treats her kindly, and at several points articulates a strong belief in God's will. "Let go, let God," "God always finds a way to give you another shot," and "God's grace is retroactive" are not maxims you hear in most mainstream films.

We learn later that Lorenzo's equanimity has come from having had some demons of his own, including a jailed son.

Matters are not helped by Brenda's hot-blooded Gannon police detective brother, Danny (Ron Eldard), with a bluntly provocative manner, prompting Lorenzo to work all the harder keeping racial tensions at bay.

Karen Collucci (a brunette Falco looking quite unlike her Carmela Soprano character), who heads a missing-children activist group -- her own child went missing years before -- offers the group's services to Lorenzo, who reluctantly accepts. The team then sets out to a long-abandoned youth center called Freedomland, located in a wooded area, where children had once been abused, hoping the terrible ghosts of the past may trigger some revelation from Brenda.

Eventually, the story of the child's disappearance will be revealed, but only after tensions between the two neighborhoods boil over into violence.

Director Joe Roth's film, based on Richard Price's bestseller, is finely acted by its two leads. As the asthmatic middle-aged detective, Jackson gives an effortlessly powerful performance, and Moore, whose real fireworks come near the end of the film, is convincingly fragile throughout. Falco also credibly limns a woman hurt by the past.

But despite such worthy themes as the futility of racial hatred and the cruelty of child abuse, a redemptive ending, and a central character imbued with a strong faith, Price's screenplay is undermined by plot contrivances and a heightened sense of hysteria that seems phony. The film has nowhere near the emotional payoff of the similarly themed "Crash."

In addition to Lorenzo's strong spirituality, there's a brief but reverent portrayal of a priest by actor Philip Bosco.

The street language used throughout, though dramatically justified given the milieu, will offend many viewers, but violence is kept to a minimum.

The film contains much profanity and rough language, racial epithets, riot violence, some blood, drug references, an intense emotional breakdown, an unwed mother, adultery, domestic and child abuse, and a fall from a window. The USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is L -- limited adult audience, films whose problematic content many adults would find troubling. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is R -- restricted. Under 17 requires accompanying parent or adult guardian.
